title: Pneumonia: Community, Healthcare Exposure, Severity, and Source
bottomLine: Pneumonia management starts with confirming a compatible lower-respiratory syndrome, assessing severity and deciding the care setting. Community-onset and hospital/healthcare-associated infection have different pathogen/resistance contexts; antibiotic breadth should follow severity, exposures, prior microbiology and local guidance rather than the label alone.
recognize: Fever, cough, sputum, pleuritic pain, dyspnea, hypoxemia and focal chest findings can support pneumonia, but older/immunocompromised patients may present atypically.
Hospital exposure, recent antibiotics, aspiration risk, structural lung disease and prior resistant organisms materially change empiric choices.
differentiate: Acute bronchitis usually lacks focal infiltrate/physiologic compromise and does not routinely benefit from antibiotics.
Pulmonary edema, PE, viral infection, COPD/asthma exacerbation, malignancy and aspiration pneumonitis can mimic pneumonia.
assessment: Assess oxygenation, work of breathing, BP/perfusion, mental status, hydration, comorbidity, aspiration risk, immune status, recent healthcare/antibiotic exposure and prior organisms.
workup: Use chest imaging when pneumonia probability/severity or disposition warrants confirmation; cultures are targeted to severe, resistant-risk or treatment-failure scenarios rather than ordered universally.
Use viral testing and other diagnostics when results will change treatment or infection-control decisions.
management: Choose outpatient versus hospital care from physiologic severity, comorbidity, ability to take oral therapy and social safety, not age alone.
Use current Canadian/local antimicrobial pathways and narrow therapy when microbiology/clinical response permit; ensure source-control or aspiration issues are addressed.
medicationSafety: Renal/hepatic function, QT risk, allergies, pregnancy and drug interactions can change antibiotic selection.
Do not extend antibiotics automatically because cough or radiographic change persists when the overall course is improving and the evidence-supported duration is complete.
counselling: Teach expected recovery, hydration/medication adherence and return precautions for worsening dyspnea, chest pain, confusion or inability to maintain intake.
followUp: Reassess unresolved or recurrent pneumonia for complications, resistant infection, aspiration or obstructing lesion rather than simply repeating antibiotics.
examTrap: Broadening antibiotics solely because the patient was recently in a healthcare setting without considering actual resistance risk, severity and prior microbiology.
oneLinePearl: Pneumonia treatment follows syndrome, severity and resistance risk—not a single setting label.
sourceBasis: Canadian Thoracic Society/Canadian infectious-disease respiratory guidance

title: Pulmonary Embolism: Diagnose by Probability, Treat by Risk
bottomLine: Suspected PE requires pretest-probability reasoning before D-dimer or imaging. Once PE is confirmed, treatment and disposition depend on hemodynamics, bleeding risk, RV strain/biomarkers and overall early-death risk; shock or persistent hypotension is a high-risk PE emergency.
recognize: Dyspnea, pleuritic chest pain, tachycardia, hypoxemia, hemoptysis, presyncope/syncope and DVT signs are compatible but nonspecific.
Provoking factors include surgery, immobilization, cancer, estrogen/pregnancy and prior VTE, while many first events are unprovoked.
differentiate: Low clinical probability can support a D-dimer-based rule-out strategy; high probability generally proceeds directly to definitive imaging rather than using D-dimer as a gate.
High-risk PE is defined by hemodynamic compromise; intermediate risk involves RV strain/biomarkers without shock and needs closer monitored assessment.
assessment: Assess BP/perfusion, oxygenation, syncope, chest pain, bleeding risk, VTE risk factors, pregnancy, renal function and anticoagulant exposure.
workup: Use validated pretest probability, D-dimer when appropriate and definitive imaging based on probability/contraindications.
After confirmed PE, assess RV strain and biomarkers when they change risk classification/disposition.
management: Start anticoagulation promptly when PE is confirmed or highly likely and bleeding risk allows, using the current Thrombosis Canada pathway.
High-risk PE requires emergency advanced therapy consideration; low-risk selected patients may be managed outpatient only when clinical/social safety criteria are met.
medicationSafety: Anticoagulant choice depends on pregnancy, cancer, renal/hepatic function, interactions and bleeding risk.
Systemic thrombolysis is not routine for every PE; benefit-risk changes sharply with hemodynamic instability and bleeding risk.
counselling: Teach anticoagulant adherence, bleeding precautions and urgent symptoms; review provoking factors and duration plan at follow-up.
followUp: Ensure duration/reassessment, malignancy/underlying-cause considerations when appropriate, and evaluation for persistent dyspnea/chronic thromboembolic disease.
examTrap: Ordering D-dimer in a high-probability patient instead of definitive imaging—or giving thrombolysis to a stable low-risk PE because the clot looks large on CT.
oneLinePearl: PE diagnosis starts with probability; PE treatment starts with hemodynamic risk.
sourceBasis: Thrombosis Canada Pulmonary Embolism Diagnosis Guide
Thrombosis Canada Pulmonary Embolism Treatment Guide
Thrombosis Canada High- and Intermediate-Risk PE Guide

title: Obstructive Sleep Apnea: Confirm the Disorder, Treat the Consequences
bottomLine: OSA is diagnosed with objective sleep testing in the correct clinical context; snoring or a screening score is not the diagnosis. Treatment is individualized to severity, symptoms, cardiovascular/occupational risk, anatomy and preference, with PAP therapy requiring adherence, interface and efficacy follow-up rather than a one-time prescription.
recognize: Loud snoring, witnessed apneas, gasping, unrefreshing sleep, daytime sleepiness, resistant hypertension, atrial fibrillation and obesity can raise suspicion.
Normal BMI does not exclude OSA, and severe OSA can present as impaired concentration, mood symptoms or driving risk rather than obvious sleepiness.
differentiate: Central sleep apnea, insomnia, circadian disorders, restless legs and medication/alcohol effects can cause sleep symptoms but require different management.
A questionnaire estimates risk; polysomnography or validated home testing establishes sleep-disordered breathing in appropriate patients.
assessment: Assess symptoms, witnessed events, sleep duration, driving/occupation, alcohol/sedatives, nasal/anatomic issues, cardiopulmonary disease and pregnancy context.
workup: Choose home sleep apnea testing versus in-lab polysomnography according to comorbidity, pretest probability and local sleep-medicine criteria.
Review event index, oxygen burden and test quality with symptoms rather than treating the index alone.
management: Use CPAP/APAP when indicated and address weight, alcohol/sedative exposure, positional factors and nasal obstruction; mandibular advancement or surgical approaches may be appropriate in selected patients.
Severe sleepiness/unsafe driving requires explicit risk counselling while treatment is established.
medicationSafety: Sedatives, opioids and alcohol can worsen sleep-disordered breathing and impairment.
Do not prescribe chronic wake-promoting medication as a substitute for optimizing OSA therapy and sleep duration.
redFlags: Heart failure/neuromuscular disease with possible central/hypoventilation syndrome
counselling: Normalize mask/interface troubleshooting and explain that adherence/comfort problems are treatable rather than proof that PAP 'failed'.
followUp: Review PAP use, residual events/leak, symptoms and equipment issues; reassess diagnosis/treatment if symptoms persist despite apparently adequate therapy.
examTrap: Diagnosing OSA from STOP-BANG alone or abandoning CPAP after one uncomfortable mask without troubleshooting adherence/interface issues.
oneLinePearl: Screening predicts OSA risk; sleep testing diagnoses it, and PAP follow-up makes treatment work.
sourceBasis: Canadian Thoracic Society/Canadian Sleep Society sleep-disordered-breathing resources

title: Pleural Effusion: Transudate, Exudate, Infection, or Malignancy?
bottomLine: Pleural effusion is a manifestation, not a diagnosis. Use history, imaging and the clinical pattern to decide whether the cause is already apparent or requires thoracentesis; when fluid is sampled, classify the process and pursue infection, malignancy or other causes rather than treating the volume alone.
recognize: Heart failure is a common transudative cause; pneumonia, malignancy, PE, TB and inflammatory disease commonly produce exudative patterns.
Fever, pleuritic pain, loculation, low pleural pH or pus raises concern for complicated parapneumonic effusion/empyema.
differentiate: Bilateral effusions in obvious decompensated HF may respond to therapy without immediate sampling; unilateral, atypical or nonresolving effusions deserve broader evaluation.
Pleural fluid cytology can support malignancy but a negative first sample does not always exclude cancer.
assessment: Assess dyspnea/hypoxemia, fever, chest pain, cancer/TB/VTE risk, heart/renal/liver disease, medications and weight loss.
workup: Use chest imaging and ultrasound; if sampled, obtain pleural/serum studies appropriate to classify the effusion and targeted pH, culture, cytology or specialized studies according to the differential.
management: Treat the cause; drain infected/complicated fluid when indicated and relieve significant symptoms when appropriate.
Persistent/recurrent unexplained or malignant effusion requires respirology/pleural-service evaluation rather than serial isolated taps.
medicationSafety: Avoid repeated antibiotics for an undiagnosed recurrent effusion solely because inflammatory markers are elevated.
Procedure-related antithrombotic decisions remain drug/risk/local-policy specific.
counselling: Explain why the clinical question determines whether fluid needs sampling or whether treating the underlying disease first is safer.
followUp: Close the loop on cytology/culture and repeat imaging when it changes management; ensure persistent unexplained effusion has specialist ownership.
examTrap: Tapping every bilateral heart-failure effusion automatically—or treating a recurrent unilateral effusion without establishing the cause.
oneLinePearl: Pleural fluid is a clue to the disease; classify the process, then treat the cause.

title: Hemoptysis: Stabilize First, Then Find the Source
bottomLine: Hemoptysis ranges from blood-streaked sputum to an airway-threatening emergency. First distinguish true pulmonary bleeding from epistaxis/GI sources and assess airway, oxygenation and hemodynamics; volume alone is less important than whether bleeding threatens ventilation or perfusion.
recognize: Common causes include infection/bronchiectasis, malignancy, anticoagulation, TB, PE and inflammatory/vascular disease.
Ongoing brisk bleeding, inability to clear secretions, hypoxemia or instability defines high-risk disease regardless of the estimated millilitres.
differentiate: Pseudohemoptysis from upper airway and hematemesis from GI bleeding have different source clues and workups.
Blood-streaked sputum in stable bronchitis is different from recurrent hemoptysis in an older smoker or patient with TB/bronchiectasis.
assessment: Assess ABCs, amount/tempo, anticoagulants, smoking/cancer/TB risk, infection, VTE risk and prior structural lung disease.
Look for unilateral breath findings, hypoxemia, anemia/shock and signs of systemic vasculitis.
workup: Use CBC/coagulation testing when indicated and chest imaging based on risk/severity; CT/CT angiography and bronchoscopy are selected according to stability/source localization.
Do not delay airway/resuscitation steps for an exhaustive outpatient workup in major bleeding.
management: Major hemoptysis requires emergency airway/critical-care/interventional assessment; position/airway strategy and definitive bronchial-artery or surgical management depend on source and severity.
Minor stable hemoptysis still requires cause-directed evaluation when recurrent or high-risk.
medicationSafety: Review anticoagulants/antiplatelets and reverse/hold only according to bleeding severity, drug and thrombotic risk.
Avoid empiric anticoagulation for suspected PE until active significant pulmonary bleeding is assessed.
counselling: Give explicit emergency return instructions for recurrent/increasing blood, dyspnea, dizziness or chest pain.
followUp: Ensure abnormal imaging and recurrent unexplained bleeding are closed-loop to respirology/ENT/oncology or other appropriate pathway.
examTrap: Using an arbitrary blood-volume cutoff to decide severity while ignoring hypoxemia, airway obstruction and hemodynamics.
oneLinePearl: Major hemoptysis is dangerous because it can drown the airway—not because a measuring cup reaches a magic number.
sourceBasis: Canadian TB and thrombosis guidance where applicable

title: Chronic Cough: Find the Pattern Before Escalating Testing
bottomLine: Chronic cough is a structured differential, not a default antibiotic diagnosis. Identify red flags and medication/smoking exposures first, then evaluate common upper-airway, asthma/eosinophilic, reflux and chronic-lung causes with targeted testing and therapeutic trials rather than ordering everything at once.
recognize: ACE inhibitors, smoking/vaping, upper-airway symptoms, asthma/eosinophilic disease and reflux are common contributors.
Multiple causes can coexist, so partial improvement after one intervention does not always end the workup.
differentiate: Hemoptysis, weight loss, persistent fever, abnormal imaging, significant dyspnea or high cancer/TB risk moves the patient off the routine chronic-cough pathway.
Postinfectious cough can persist for weeks but should improve rather than progressively worsen.
assessment: Ask duration, triggers, nocturnal/exertional pattern, sputum/hemoptysis, upper-airway/reflux symptoms, medications, smoking/vaping/cannabis, occupational exposure and systemic red flags.
workup: Use chest radiograph and spirometry when indicated by duration/risk; add targeted eosinophilic, sinus, reflux, CT or specialist evaluation only when the clinical pathway supports it.
Do not order routine CT/bronchoscopy in every patient with normal initial assessment and no red flags.
management: Stop an ACE inhibitor when clinically appropriate and assess response; treat identified asthma/upper-airway/reflux or exposure drivers with evidence-based therapy.
Refer persistent unexplained cough, abnormal imaging or significant functional impairment for specialty evaluation.
medicationSafety: Avoid repeated antibiotics, opioids or sedating cough suppressants without a defined indication.
Check interactions and fall/respiratory risk before centrally acting antitussives.
counselling: Explain that chronic cough often has several treatable contributors and that improvement may require staged reassessment.
followUp: Set a response checkpoint after each targeted intervention; if the expected response does not occur, revisit the differential rather than simply adding more therapy.
examTrap: Giving a third antibiotic for a chronic cough with normal vitals and no bacterial syndrome instead of reviewing ACE inhibitors, asthma, upper airway and reflux causes.
oneLinePearl: Chronic cough is solved by pattern and staged testing—not serial antibiotics.
sourceBasis: Choosing Wisely Canada respiratory diagnostic stewardship

title: Tuberculosis: Infection Is Not Disease, and Disease Is a Public-Health Diagnosis
bottomLine: TB infection testing identifies immune sensitization, not active disease. Before treating TB infection, exclude active TB when symptoms/risk warrant it; suspected pulmonary TB disease requires appropriate airborne precautions, microbiologic evaluation and public-health/specialist coordination.
recognize: Pulmonary TB can cause chronic cough, fever/night sweats, weight loss and hemoptysis but may be subtle, especially with immune compromise.
Risk is shaped by exposure, country/region epidemiology, congregate settings, immune suppression and social/structural determinants.
differentiate: A positive TST/IGRA cannot distinguish latent TB infection from active TB disease.
BCG vaccination affects TST interpretation in some contexts but does not explain away a positive IGRA.
assessment: Assess symptoms, exposure history, prior TB/testing/treatment, immune status, pregnancy, medications/interactions, country/travel and barriers to completing therapy.
workup: Use TST or IGRA only when the result will change management and follow the Canadian TB Standards for selection/interpretation.
Suspected pulmonary TB disease requires chest imaging and appropriate respiratory specimens for molecular/microscopy/culture testing; follow infection-control/public-health pathways.
management: Treat active TB with a specialist/public-health coordinated multidrug regimen after appropriate diagnostic sampling when feasible.
TB preventive treatment is offered after active disease is reasonably excluded, using a current Canadian regimen matched to interactions, pregnancy, age and adherence considerations.
medicationSafety: TB therapies have important hepatotoxicity and drug-interaction considerations; rifamycins can substantially alter exposure to many drugs.
Do not start single-drug latent-TB therapy in a patient who may have active TB disease.
counselling: Use culturally safe, non-stigmatizing language and explain the difference between infection and contagious disease.
Coordinate adherence supports and public-health contact management.
followUp: Ensure public-health notification/contact investigation when required and monitor treatment adherence/toxicity to completion.
examTrap: Calling a positive IGRA 'active TB' or starting latent-TB monotherapy before excluding active disease in a symptomatic patient.
oneLinePearl: TST/IGRA detect infection; sputum/imaging and the clinical syndrome diagnose TB disease.
sourceBasis: Canadian Tuberculosis Standards, 8th edition — diagnosis of TB disease and infection, treatment and prevention

title: Lung Cancer Screening: Screening Is Not Symptom Evaluation
bottomLine: Lung-cancer screening is for eligible asymptomatic people using the current provincial program/risk pathway. Hemoptysis, weight loss, persistent focal symptoms or another cancer concern requires diagnostic evaluation, not entry into a screening algorithm.
recognize: Eligibility and implementation differ across Canadian provincial programs and can use age plus smoking/risk-model criteria.
Low-dose CT screening reduces mortality in selected high-risk populations but also creates false positives and incidental findings requiring structured follow-up.
differentiate: Screening low-dose CT is not the correct test pathway for a symptomatic patient.
An incidental pulmonary nodule found outside a screening program follows an incidental-nodule management pathway, which is not identical to a screening-program algorithm.
assessment: Confirm absence/presence of symptoms, smoking history, age/risk criteria, prior cancer/imaging, ability/willingness to pursue follow-up and local program availability.
workup: Use the current provincial/territorial screening program or validated Canadian risk pathway; do not invent one universal Canada-wide interval.
Switch to diagnostic imaging/referral when symptoms or high-risk clinical findings are present.
management: Enroll eligible asymptomatic patients in an organized screening program where available and provide smoking-cessation support.
Ensure abnormal screens/nodules have closed-loop follow-up through the appropriate pathway.
medicationSafety: Avoid unnecessary contrast/invasive testing before the screening/nodule pathway supports it.
counselling: Discuss potential benefit, false positives, incidental findings and the commitment to follow-up rather than presenting screening as a one-time reassurance test.
followUp: Use program-defined recall and ensure diagnostic resolution of abnormal screens; unresolved abnormal findings must not be lost to follow-up.
examTrap: Ordering a screening LDCT for a patient with hemoptysis instead of initiating a diagnostic cancer workup.
oneLinePearl: No symptoms means screening; symptoms mean diagnosis.

title: Respiratory Infection in the Immunocompromised Host
bottomLine: Immunocompromised patients can have dangerous lower-respiratory infection with little fever or an initially unrevealing chest radiograph. Define the immune defect, severity and prophylaxis, broaden the differential beyond routine CAP, obtain appropriate imaging/microbiology early and escalate unstable patients before waiting for a classic presentation.
recognize: Neutropenia, transplant, hematologic malignancy, targeted/biologic therapy, prolonged high-dose corticosteroids and advanced immune deficiency create different pathogen risks.
Hypoxemia, tachypnea, confusion or hemodynamic change can be more important than fever or WBC response.
differentiate: Bacterial pneumonia is only one possibility; viral, Pneumocystis, fungal, mycobacterial and noninfectious drug/immune lung injury can overlap.
Normal early radiography or absent leukocytosis does not safely exclude serious disease in a high-risk host.
assessment: Define the immune defect, timing of treatment/transplant, prophylaxis, neutrophil count where relevant, prior organisms, travel/exposures, oxygenation and medication toxicity risks.
workup: Use prompt chest imaging and targeted bacterial/viral/fungal/mycobacterial testing; obtain cultures before antimicrobials when feasible without delaying therapy in an unstable patient.
Early specialist input and bronchoscopy/BAL may be required when diagnosis is unclear or disease severe.
management: High-risk or unstable patients need hospital-level assessment and empiric therapy matched to immune defect, local epidemiology and prior microbiology, with de-escalation when evidence permits.
Do not treat a transplant recipient or neutropenic patient with progressive respiratory symptoms as routine outpatient CAP.
medicationSafety: Antifungals, antivirals, transplant and oncology drugs have important renal/hepatic and interaction risks.
Avoid reflex corticosteroid escalation for presumed inflammatory lung disease until serious infection has been considered.
redFlags: Suspected invasive fungal or Pneumocystis infection
counselling: Teach early contact thresholds because severe infection can present without typical fever or sputum change.
followUp: Close the loop on microbiology and revise therapy promptly; coordinate transplant/oncology/infectious-disease/respirology follow-up.
examTrap: Reassuring a severely immunocompromised patient because they are afebrile and the first chest radiograph is normal.
oneLinePearl: Immunosuppression can mute inflammation without reducing infection danger.
